← Invoice payment terms calculator

FOR FREELANCERS AND SMALL SERVICE FIRMS

It is already late. Now what?

The due-date calculator prices an invoice that gets paid on terms. This one starts after that date has passed. Score the same overdue invoice four ways — keep waiting, chase it yourself, offer a settlement, or hand it to a collection agency — on the cash each is worth once you price the odds, the wait, and the hours chasing it costs you.

The invoice

Keep waiting

Chase it yourself

Offer a settlement

Send to collections

What each path is worth

—

Expected value = odds × (cash after float) − hours spent
PathCash if paidOddsWorth

Where each path flips

Why chasing an invoice yourself so often loses

Chasing recovers the most cash of any path when it works — you give up no discount and no commission. What sinks it is that the hours are certain and the payment is not. On the defaults, three hours at $85 is $255 spent whether or not the client ever pays, which drops an 85% chance at $1,188.95 down to $755.61. A 10% settlement paid in five days at 80% odds is worth $861.16.

That is why the chase-hours break-even is the most useful number on the page. At these defaults it is about 1.8 hours: one focused call and a firm email is worth it, six weeks of polite follow-ups is not. If you can make the chase cheap — a scheduled reminder, a statement, one call — the arithmetic changes in its favour, and you can watch it change by typing fewer hours.

PathCash if paidWaitOddsYour timeWorth
Offer a settlement$1,080.005 days80%$0.00$861.16
Keep waiting$1,200.0030 days70%$0.00$823.43
Chase it yourself$1,200.0014 days85%$255.00$755.61
Send to collections$840.0090 days45%$0.00$355.63

What these numbers are not

The odds are your estimate of this client, not a prediction — the calculator has never met them. Carrying cost is the rate you type, not a late fee and not interest you can invoice; use the main calculator for late-fee scenarios. Whether a late fee is permitted, what a collection agency may do, and what a settlement means for a balance you still intend to pursue are legal questions that vary by jurisdiction and by the contract you signed. This page does not answer them, and it does not tell you to settle, escalate, or walk away.

Common questions

Is it worth chasing a late invoice yourself?

It depends on how many of your own hours it takes, because those hours are spent whether or not you get paid. On the calculator defaults — a $1,200 invoice 15 days overdue, 85% odds of recovery, $85 an hour — chasing recovers the most cash of any path if it works, but three hours of your time costs $255 and drops it to $755.61. It only gets ahead of a 10% settlement if you can close it in under about 1.8 hours.

How much do collection agencies take?

Commissions on small commercial invoices are commonly quoted in the 25-50% range, and the calculator defaults to 30% over 90 days at 45% odds. On a $1,200 invoice that is worth $355.63 — behind every other path. It gets more interesting on a large invoice from a payer unlikely to settle: at $20,000 with 55% odds, collections leads and stays ahead up to about a 65% commission. Enter the commission you were actually quoted.

Should I offer a discount to settle an overdue invoice?

The calculator prices it rather than recommending it. On the defaults a 10% settlement paid in 5 days at 80% odds is worth $861.16, which is $37.73 more than waiting. The break-even is about 13.9% — past that, waiting is worth more on these odds. This is arithmetic from numbers you type, not a recommendation to settle.

Before you send the first invoice: how should the project be split?

Everything above prices one invoice. This prices the schedule — how much of your finished work is sitting unpaid on the day you hand it over, and how much of the client's project you are financing until they pay. It uses the payment terms and carrying-cost rate you set above.

Schedule Unpaid at handover Peak unpaid Paid in full (day) Financing cost

“Unpaid at handover” is the finished work still outstanding the day you deliver — what you lose if the client never pays. Only money that has cleared before that day counts, so an invoice sent at completion never protects you, however large.

Delivered value is assumed to spread evenly across the project's days; front-loaded work is exposed more than this shows. These are arithmetic scenarios from the numbers you enter, not a recommendation to ask for a deposit and not a prediction about any client.

Common questions

When is a Net 30 invoice due?

On the calculator defaults a $1,200 invoice dated today with 30-day terms is due 30 days later. Three similar invoices outstanding are $3,600 of exposure — 36 operating days at a $3,000 monthly burn.

Should I offer 2/10 Net 30?

On a $1,200 invoice, 2% for payment in 10 days leaves $1,168.27 after 24% carrying cost. Waiting 30 days for the full $1,200 leaves $1,176.33 — $8.06 ahead. They match at about 36.1%. This is not a recommendation to offer or withhold the discount.

Should I factor this invoice?

On a $1,200 invoice, a 3% factor fee with a 90% advance leaves $1,161.24 after 24% carrying cost. Waiting 30 days leaves $1,176.33 — $15.09 ahead. They match at a 1.74% fee. This is not a recommendation to factor or to wait.

Should I ask for a deposit?

On a $6,000 project delivered over 30 days with Net 30 paid 12 days late, billing once at the end leaves $6,000 of finished work unpaid on handover day and costs $224.88 to finance at 24%. A 50% deposit that clears in 5 days leaves $3,000 unpaid and costs $99.29. A deposit collected on the same 42-day cycle leaves all $6,000 unpaid — the collection time protects you, not the percentage. This is not a recommendation to ask for a deposit.

Does this make a late fee enforceable?

No. Late-fee rows are arithmetic scenarios from the annual rate and grace period you type. They are not legal advice and do not determine whether a fee is permitted.

Why does my invoice get paid after the due date even when the client is not late?

Most accounts-payable departments pay in runs rather than on the day each invoice falls due — weekdays only, the 1st and 15th, once a month, or one weekday a week. An invoice dated 2026-08-24 on Net 30 is due 2026-09-23, but at a client who pays on the 1st and 15th the cash lands 2026-10-01: eight days of drift the due date never shows, costing about $6.31 on $1,200 at a 24% carrying rate.

Is Net 45 more expensive than Net 30?

Not always. Because payment runs are batched, a longer term often lands on the very same run. At a client paying once a month on the 1st, an invoice dated 2026-08-24 lands 2026-10-01 under both Net 15 and Net 30 — fifteen extra days of terms at no cost in cash timing. The calculator compares Net 7, 15, 30, 45, and 60 side by side so you can see where that happens.

should-i-ask-for-a-deposit.html.text:
← Invoice payment terms calculator

Should I ask for a deposit?

Freelancers search this after a project goes wrong — the work shipped, the invoice went out, and the money did not arrive. The usual answer is a percentage: ask for 50%, ask for a third. The percentage is the wrong thing to argue about.

What matters is whether the deposit clears before you finish. A deposit that lands after handover is not protection. It is a slightly cheaper way to finance the same risk.

The defaults: a $6,000 project over 30 days

Net 30, paid 12 days late (so 42 days from invoice to cash), a deposit that clears in 5 days because nobody starts before it does, and money worth 24% a year. “Unpaid at handover” is the finished work still outstanding on delivery day — what a client who disappears keeps.

ScheduleUnpaid at handoverFinancing cost
50% deposit, 50% on completion$3,000.00$99.29
Thirds: deposit, midpoint, completion$3,960.00$117.25
Bill once at the end$6,000.00$224.88

Billing once at the end means the entire $6,000 of delivered work is in someone else's hands on the day you let go of it, and stays there until day 72. The half deposit cuts that to $3,000 and the financing cost to $99.29.

Thirds is worse than a half deposit here

This is the result that surprises people, and it is why the schedule is worth checking rather than copying. Thirds leaves $3,960 unpaid at handover against the half deposit's $3,000 — more invoices, more exposure.

The midpoint bill is issued on day 15 and collected on the same 42-day cycle as everything else, so it lands on day 57: nearly a month after the work was delivered. It splits the money into smaller pieces without moving any of it in front of the handover, and the smaller deposit (34% instead of 50%) is all that actually arrives in time. A progress bill only helps if it clears while the project is still running.

A slow deposit protects nothing at all

Change one number — the deposit takes 42 days to collect, like every other invoice — and the whole table collapses: every schedule leaves the full $6,000 unpaid at handover. Nothing clears inside a 30-day project.

The 50% on the contract did not disappear; it never mattered. What protected the freelancer in the first table was five days, not fifty percent. On this version the 50% deposit is worth $59.18 of financing and exactly zero risk, and the fix is a shorter collection cycle — payable on acceptance, before work starts — not a bigger number on the same terms.

Working the percentage backwards

If you know the most you are willing to have unpaid, the calculator solves for the deposit instead. On the defaults, holding peak unpaid work at or below $2,000 takes a 66.67% deposit.

There is a floor it cannot get under. Until the deposit clears you have delivered five days of a thirty-day project and been paid nothing, so no percentage — not even 100% — pushes the peak below $1,000. Ask for a ceiling under that and the answer is that no deposit reaches it, which is more useful than a number above 100% that reads like a target.

What this does not tell you

It does not say to ask for a deposit, and it is not a prediction that any particular client will pay late or not at all. Delivered value is assumed to spread evenly across the project's days; if your work is front-loaded, your real exposure is worse than these figures. A client who has prepaid is not treated as lending you money, so a large deposit never manufactures a gain — it only removes a cost.

Run it on your own project →

Should I offer 2/10 Net 30? answers the other half: once the invoice is out, what is speed worth?

Common questions

Should I ask for a deposit?

On the calculator defaults — a $6,000 project delivered over 30 days, Net 30 paid 12 days late, and a deposit that clears in 5 days — billing once at the end leaves $6,000 of finished work unpaid on the day you hand it over, and costs $224.88 to finance at a 24% carrying-cost assumption. A 50% deposit leaves $3,000 unpaid and costs $99.29. This is arithmetic from the numbers you enter, not a recommendation to ask for a deposit and not a prediction about any client.

Does a deposit protect me if the client pays it slowly?

No. Set the deposit to collect in 42 days instead of 5 and every schedule leaves the full $6,000 unpaid at handover, because no invoice clears inside a 30-day project. The 50% on the contract is not what protects you; the deposit arriving before you finish the work is. On a short project a slow deposit is a discount on your financing cost and nothing more — the 50% split cuts financing from $224.88 to $165.70 and moves the exposure by zero.

Is a three-way split safer than a 50% deposit?

Not necessarily, and on these defaults it is worse. Thirds leaves $3,960 unpaid at handover against $3,000 for a straight half deposit, because the midpoint bill is issued on day 15 and collected on the 42-day cycle — it lands on day 57, nearly a month after the work was delivered. More invoices only help when the extra invoices clear before handover.

What deposit percentage do I need?

It depends on the most you are willing to have unpaid. On the defaults, holding peak unpaid work at or below $2,000 needs a 66.67% deposit. Below the work you deliver before the deposit itself clears, no percentage reaches the target — the calculator says so rather than printing a figure above 100%.

should-i-factor-this-invoice.html.text:
← Invoice payment terms calculator

Should I factor this invoice?

Freelancers search this after a factor, a card “get paid now” button, or a bookkeeper suggests selling the receivable. Three percent off a $1,200 invoice looks cheap until you price the fee against the cash you were going to wait 30 days for.

This is not 2/10 Net 30. That discount is money you give the client. Factoring is a fee you pay a third party. The client still has Net 30. You get an advance today and a reserve after they pay.

On the calculator defaults — $1,200, 3% fee, 90% advance, reserve on day 35, 24% money — the factor takes $36.00 and advances $1,044.00 today. The $120 reserve arrives later. Factoring leaves $1,161.24. Waiting 30 days for $1,200 leaves $1,176.33 — $15.09 ahead. They match at a 1.74% fee, or about 41.3% money.

At 50%, the same fee leaves $1,158.25 and waiting leaves $1,150.68. A 1.5% fee at 24% flips ahead by $2.91. Cheap 6% money still covers the wait by about $31.

Path Cash now Later After float vs wait

Carrying cost is your assumption, not a late fee and not interest you can invoice. The factor fee, advance, and reserve dates come from the quote you actually have — this page does not publish a factor’s live schedule. Complementary to Should I offer 2/10 Net 30? (a discount you give the client). Open the invoice payment terms calculator to change the amount.

Common questions

Should I factor this invoice or wait for Net 30?

On the calculator defaults — a $1,200 invoice, a 3% factor fee, a 90% advance, a 35-day reserve, and a 24% annual carrying-cost assumption — factoring leaves $1,161.24 after the $36.00 fee. Waiting 30 days for $1,200 leaves $1,176.33. The fee is larger than the float you skip. This is not a recommendation to factor or to wait.

When does invoice factoring still beat waiting?

When your money is expensive or the fee is cheap. At a 50% annual carrying-cost assumption the same invoice leaves $1,158.25 after factoring and $1,150.68 after waiting. Factoring and waiting match at a 1.74% fee or about 41.3% money. A 1.5% fee at 24% flips ahead by $2.91.

Is factoring the same as offering 2/10 Net 30?

No. 2/10 is a discount you give the client to pay faster. Factoring is a fee you pay a third party while the client still has Net 30. The 2/10 page prices the discount. This page prices the factor fee, the advance, and the reserve.

should-i-offer-2-10-net-30.html.text:
← Invoice payment terms calculator

Should I offer 2/10 Net 30?

Freelancers search this after a client asks for a discount to pay faster, or after they copy “2/10 Net 30” from someone else’s invoice. Two percent off for payment in ten days looks cheap until you price the cash you give up against the cash you wait for.

The discount is $24. The wait is 20 days. On the calculator defaults — a $1,200 invoice, 2% for payment in 10 days, Net 30 for the full amount — early cash is $1,176.00. Waiting pays $1,200.00.

24% money still leaves waiting ahead. A card or operating line at 24% models $7.73 of carrying cost on the $1,176 you could have on day 10, and $23.67 on the $1,200 you wait 30 days for. Early-pay leaves $1,168.27. Waiting leaves $1,176.33 — $8.06 ahead. They match at about 36.1%.

Expensive capital flips the table. At 50%, the same discount leaves $1,159.89 and waiting leaves $1,150.68. Cheap 6% money still covers the wait by about $20.

Path Wait Cash Carrying at 24% After float
2% / 10 days10 days$1,176.00$7.73$1,168.27
Wait Net 3030 days$1,200.00$23.67$1,176.33

What this number is not

Carrying cost is your assumption, not a late fee and not interest you can invoice. The 37.2% APR is the buyer’s annualized cost of skipping the discount, not a rate you charge. Confirm any term against the contract you actually send. This page does not tell you to offer or withhold 2/10 Net 30.

A third-party factor fee is a different question — Should I factor this invoice? prices the advance, not a discount you give the client. A Faire marketplace Pay Now discount is also a different question — Should I offer Faire Pay Now? prices a brand-funded early-pay percent against Faire remittance wait, with no client Net 30 invoice in the middle. Open the invoice payment terms calculator, type your own rate, and see whether the discount still covers the wait.

Common questions

Should I offer 2/10 Net 30?

On the calculator defaults — a $1,200 invoice, 2% off for payment in 10 days, and a 24% annual carrying-cost assumption — the discount leaves $1,168.27 after $7.73 of modeled float. Waiting 30 days for $1,200 leaves $1,176.33. The $24.00 discount does not cover 24% money sitting the extra 20 days. This is not a recommendation to offer or withhold the discount.

When does a 2/10 discount still beat waiting?

When your money is expensive. At a 50% annual carrying-cost assumption the same invoice leaves $1,159.89 after the discount and $1,150.68 after waiting. Early-pay and waiting match at about 36.1%. Enter the rate you actually pay on a card, line, or opportunity cost.

What is the 2/10 Net 30 APR?

Giving up 2% to keep the cash 20 extra days is about 37.2% annualized for the buyer. That is the cost of not taking the discount, not a rate you can invoice and not a reason to offer it.

vs-freshbooks.html.text:
← Invoice payment terms calculator

This calculator vs. FreshBooks

Two different shapes: FreshBooks is paid invoicing and bookkeeping software you sign up for and use as an ongoing system of record. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — given this invoice's terms and how your client actually runs payments, when does the cash land, and does an early-pay discount or factoring beat waiting.

FreshBooks sends and tracks invoices, lets you set payment terms per invoice, sends automatic reminders for a late payment, accepts online payment from the client, and produces the books an accountant or tax filing needs, as a paid ongoing subscription with signup and setup. FreshBooks' own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's plan names or figures, so no dollar amount for FreshBooks appears anywhere on this page — only its well-documented identity and category (invoicing and bookkeeping software sold as a subscription, aimed at freelancers and small service businesses) are stated.

This calculator does not send an invoice, track a client's balance, or touch your books, and it stores nothing on a server. It takes an invoice amount, payment terms, and how your client's accounts-payable run actually works (weekdays only, twice a month, once a month), and turns that into the due date, the date cash actually lands once that run is accounted for, what 30/60/90 days of delay costs at your carrying-rate assumption, whether a 2/10 Net 30 discount or a factoring fee still beats waiting, and how exposed a project is under a given deposit or milestone schedule. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

What this page is not

This calculator is not a replacement for FreshBooks, or for invoicing and bookkeeping software generally. It does not send an invoice, does not track a client's running balance, and does not produce books for an accountant or a tax filing. Most freelancers who invoice regularly get different value from each: FreshBooks (or a comparable platform) for sending invoices, reminding clients, and taking online payment as an ongoing subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to when a specific invoice's cash actually arrives and whether an early-pay or factoring offer is worth taking before you set the term.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or FreshBooks?

They do different jobs and most freelancers who invoice regularly will end up using both. FreshBooks is paid invoicing and bookkeeping software built for freelancers and small service businesses: it sends the invoice, tracks who owes what across every client, accepts online payment, and produces the books an accountant or tax filing needs, sold as an ongoing subscription with a signup and setup step. This calculator does one narrower thing before or alongside that: starting from an invoice amount, payment terms, and how your client actually runs payments (weekdays, twice a month, once a month), it works out the due date, the date cash actually lands once that payment run is taken into account, what a 30/60/90-day delay costs at your carrying-cost assumption, whether a 2/10 Net 30 discount still beats waiting, whether factoring still beats waiting after the fee, and how much of a project stays unpaid under a given deposit or milestone schedule. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, sends nothing you type anywhere, and does not send the invoice itself. A freelancer who already needs one system tracking every client, every invoice, and the books behind them is better served by FreshBooks or a comparable platform; someone who wants an instant, private answer to when this invoice's cash actually arrives and whether an early-pay or factoring offer is worth it is in the right place here.

Does FreshBooks already do this?

FreshBooks lets you set payment terms per invoice, send automatic late-payment reminders, and see which invoices are outstanding or overdue. What it does not do is model when your client's specific payment run actually pays that due date, price a 2/10 early-pay discount or a factoring fee against your own cost of carrying the cash, or turn a project's billing schedule into a day-by-day unpaid-exposure figure. This calculator is not a replacement for FreshBooks' invoice tracking; it is the arithmetic step before you set the term or decide whether an early-pay or factoring offer is worth taking.

Is this page affiliated with FreshBooks?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by FreshBooks. FreshBooks is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

It does not send an invoice, does not track a client's running balance, and does not produce books for an accountant or a tax filing. Most freelancers and small firms that invoice regularly get different value from each: QuickBooks Online (or a comparable platform) for sending invoices, tracking balances, and keeping the books as an ongoing subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to when a specific invoice's cash actually arrives and whether an early-pay or factoring offer is worth taking before you set the term.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or QuickBooks Online?

They do different jobs and most freelancers who invoice regularly will end up using both. QuickBooks Online, made by Intuit, is paid bookkeeping and invoicing software: it sends the invoice, tracks who owes what across every client, reconciles bank feeds, and produces the books an accountant or tax filing needs, sold as an ongoing subscription with a signup and setup step. This calculator does one narrower thing before or alongside that: starting from an invoice amount, payment terms, and how your client actually runs payments (weekdays, twice a month, once a month), it works out the due date, the date cash actually lands once that payment run is taken into account, what a 30/60/90-day delay costs at your carrying-cost assumption, whether a 2/10 Net 30 discount still beats waiting, whether factoring still beats waiting after the fee, and how much of a project stays unpaid under a given deposit or milestone schedule. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, sends nothing you type anywhere, and does not send the invoice itself. A freelancer or small firm that already needs one system tracking every client, every invoice, and the books behind them is better served by QuickBooks Online or a comparable accounting platform; someone who wants an instant, private answer to when this invoice's cash actually arrives and whether an early-pay or factoring offer is worth it is in the right place here.

Does QuickBooks Online already do this?

QuickBooks Online lets you set payment terms (Net 15, Net 30, due on receipt, or a custom term) per customer or per invoice, and it tracks which invoices are open and how many days overdue they are. What it does not do is model when your client's specific payment run actually pays that due date, price a 2/10 early-pay discount or a factoring fee against your own cost of carrying the cash, or turn a project's billing schedule into a day-by-day unpaid-exposure figure. This calculator is not a replacement for QuickBooks Online's invoice tracking; it is the arithmetic step before you set the term or decide whether an early-pay or factoring offer is worth taking.

Is this page affiliated with QuickBooks or Intuit?

vs-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Invoice payment terms calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A freelancer who sets payment terms more than once usually ends up with a spreadsheet: an invoice date, a terms column, and a formula that adds the two. That formula gives you the invoice's due date. It does not, on its own, tell you when the cash actually lands — and for a client that only runs payments on certain days, those are often different dates. This page names no specific product; it compares against the generic method of tracking terms in a spreadsheet or by hand.

A spreadsheet can add an invoice date to a terms count in one formula, and many freelancers already have one. What it does not do on its own is model which weekday, or which day of the month, a specific client's accounts-payable system actually pays on — so a due date that falls between two payment runs silently waits for the next one, and nothing in a plain date-add formula flags that drift or prices what it costs.

This calculator takes the invoice date, the terms, and the client's stated pay-run schedule (weekdays only, twice a month, once a month on a set day, or once a week), and works out the date cash actually lands, how many days that drifts past the stated due date, what that drift costs at your own carrying-cost rate, and whether dating the invoice a few days earlier would catch an earlier run and get you paid sooner for free. It also carries the early-pay and factoring break-even math through the same pay-run projection, so a 2/10 Net 30 offer or a factoring fee is compared against when the money would actually arrive, not just the due date on the invoice.

QuestionWhere to answer it
When is this invoice due, by its stated terms?Either one — invoice date plus terms is the same formula both use.
When does the cash actually land, given this client's pay-run schedule?This calculator's pay-run projection — a plain date-add formula has no way to know a client only pays on the 1st and 15th.
What does that drift cost at my own carrying-cost rate?This calculator, priced automatically once you set a rate.
Would dating the invoice a few days earlier catch an earlier payment run?This calculator flags it when the earlier run buys more days than it costs; a spreadsheet only tells you this if you build and maintain that comparison yourself.
Does a 2/10 Net 30 discount or a factoring fee still beat waiting for the actual landing date?This calculator's early-pay and factoring comparisons, run against the same pay-run projection.
I already have a working terms sheet and don't want to change tools.Keep it — this calculator is a free second check, not a replacement for a system you maintain.

What this page is not

This calculator is not a bookkeeping system and does not track multiple clients or invoices over time; a spreadsheet or an invoicing platform still does that job better. What it replaces is the one-off arithmetic of projecting a specific client's actual pay date from their stated schedule and pricing the drift — the part of a terms sheet most likely to be approximated as "due date equals paid date" because modeling weekday-only, semimonthly, or monthly pay runs by hand, correctly, for every invoice, is tedious enough that most spreadsheets skip it.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet work out when an invoice is due?

Yes — =invoice_date+terms_days is one formula and most freelancers already have it somewhere. What that formula gives you is the due date the invoice states, not the date the money actually arrives. Accounts-payable departments run payments in batches: weekdays only, twice a month, once a month on a set day, or once a week — and a due date that lands between two runs waits for the next one. A plain date-add formula has no way to know which schedule a given client uses, so it is silently wrong on any client that does not pay same-day.

Where does a hand-built invoice-terms sheet usually go wrong?

Two places. First, treating the due date as the pay date — a Net 30 invoice due on a Saturday, or due the 16th at a client who only runs payments on the 1st and 15th, does not get paid on the due date; it waits for the next run, and that drift is real carrying cost at whatever rate the freelancer's own cash is worth. Second, re-deriving the early-pay or factoring break-even by hand every time terms or a client's discount offer changes, which is exactly the kind of repeated formula work a copied cell silently gets wrong on one row.

What does a spreadsheet not check for you?

Whether the due date actually falls on a day the client's accounts-payable system pays, and by how many days it drifts if not; whether a 2/10 Net 30 discount or a factoring fee still beats waiting once that drift and your own carrying-cost rate are priced in; and whether dating the invoice a few days earlier would catch an earlier payment run and get you paid sooner for no cost. None of those are hard formulas individually, but stacking all of them correctly, for every client's schedule, on every invoice, is where a hand-built sheet drifts.

Does either one know whether my client will actually pay on time?

No. Both this calculator and a spreadsheet model the schedule you tell them about — the stated payment terms and the client's stated pay-run cadence. Neither predicts whether a specific client pays on time, disputes the invoice, or pays late anyway.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you type is uploaded.
